docs.title: EE3601 — Transmission Lines, Fields, and Waves
docs.text: Credits: 3 (3 lecture hours per week) Level: Undergraduate, junior year Prerequisites: Circuit analysis I and II; vector calculus (multivariable calculus); university physics II (electricity and magnetism) Corequisite (recommended): Differential equations

docs.title: Catalog Description
docs.text: An introduction to electromagnetic fields and waves for electrical engineers, starting with transmission lines and building up to Maxwell's equations and plane waves. Topics include wave propagation on transmission lines, impedance matching and the Smith chart, transients on lines, electrostatics and magnetostatics, Maxwell's equations, uniform plane waves, reflection and transmission at boundaries, and an introduction to waveguides and antennas. Applications cover high-speed digital interconnects, RF and microwave circuits, and wireless and optical systems.

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text: At high frequencies, or when interconnects are long relative to the signal's wavelength, ordinary circuit theory stops working: voltage and current turn into traveling waves. EE3601 bridges circuit analysis and field theory. It starts with transmission lines, where wave behavior can be studied with familiar circuit quantities, and then develops the field theory underneath it. Students learn to analyze, design and match transmission-line circuits and to predict how electromagnetic waves propagate, reflect and transmit in practical engineering systems.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
1. Introduction to waves and phasors. Traveling waves, wavelength, phase velocity; when circuit theory breaks down; review of phasors and complex numbers.
  2. Transmission-line theory. Distributed-element model; telegrapher's equations; characteristic impedance; propagation constant; lossless and low-loss lines.
  3. Terminated transmission lines. Reflection coefficient; standing waves and VSWR; input impedance; short-circuited, open-circuited and quarter-wave lines; power flow.
  4. The Smith chart and impedance matching. Smith chart construction and use; lumped-element (L-section) matching; single-stub matching; quarter-wave transformers.
  5. Transients on transmission lines. Step and pulse response; bounce diagrams; reflections in digital interconnects and signal integrity.
  6. Vector analysis review. Coordinate systems; gradient, divergence and curl; the divergence and Stokes theorems.
  7. Electrostatics. Coulomb's law; Gauss's law; electric potential; conductors and dielectrics; boundary conditions; capacitance; Laplace's and Poisson's equations.
  8. Magnetostatics. Biot–Savart law; Ampère's law; magnetic flux and vector potential; magnetic materials; inductance.
  9. Maxwell's equations. Faraday's law; displacement current; Maxwell's equations in integral and differential (point) form; time-harmonic fields; boundary conditions.
  10. Uniform plane waves. The wave equation; propagation in lossless and lossy media; skin depth; polarization; the Poynting vector and power density.
  11. Reflection and transmission of plane waves. Normal and oblique incidence; Snell's law; Fresnel coefficients; total internal reflection; Brewster angle.
  12. Introduction to waveguides and antennas. Rectangular waveguides, TE and TM modes, and cutoff frequency; radiation from a Hertzian dipole; basic antenna parameters.

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
To keep the course focused, the following are left to later electives:

  • Antenna arrays, antenna synthesis and detailed antenna design (only the Hertzian dipole and basic antenna parameters are covered)
  • Numerical electromagnetics (FDTD, method of moments, finite element method), apart from using a field solver as a tool
  • Optical fiber modes and photonics beyond plane-wave reflection and refraction
  • Circular and dielectric waveguides, and resonant cavities
  • Microwave network theory beyond impedance matching (S-parameter network analysis, couplers, filters, amplifiers)
  • Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) regulation and shielding design
  • Relativistic electrodynamics and quantum electrodynamics

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: Students use Python (NumPy and Matplotlib) for computation and plotting, an interactive Smith chart tool, a 2-D field solver, and, where lab equipment is available, a time-domain reflectometer (TDR) and a vector network analyzer (VNA).

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Recall the values and units of the free-space constants ε₀, μ₀, the speed of light c, and the intrinsic impedance of free space η₀ ≈ 377 Ω.
  2. State Maxwell's equations in integral and differential form, together with the constitutive relations.
  3. Identify the parts of a Smith chart: constant-resistance circles, constant-reactance arcs, and the wavelength scales.
  4. Name common transmission-line types (coaxial, two-wire, microstrip, stripline) and their typical characteristic impedances.
  5. List the boundary conditions for electric and magnetic fields at an interface between two media.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why circuit theory fails when an interconnect is long compared with a wavelength or a signal's rise time.
  2. Interpret standing-wave patterns in terms of incident and reflected waves.
  3. Explain the physical meaning of each of Maxwell's equations, including displacement current.
  4. Describe how uniform plane waves propagate in lossless and lossy media, including attenuation, skin depth, polarization and power density.
  5. Explain guided-wave propagation in waveguides, including cutoff, and the basic principles of radiation from antennas.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Calculate the voltage, current, impedance, reflection coefficient, VSWR and power flow on terminated transmission lines.
  2. Use the Smith chart to find input impedances and to design lumped-element, single-stub and quarter-wave matching networks.
  3. Apply Gauss's, Ampère's and Faraday's laws to find static and time-varying fields and to calculate capacitance and inductance.
  4. Calculate the reflection and transmission of plane waves at boundaries between media, for both normal and oblique incidence.
  5. Compute the cutoff frequencies of the TE and TM modes of a rectangular waveguide.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Analyze transient signals on transmission lines with bounce diagrams and explain how reflections affect signal integrity.
  2. Choose a Gaussian surface or Amperian loop by examining a problem's symmetry.
  3. Separate the propagation constant of a lossy line or medium into its attenuation and phase contributions, and identify the dominant loss mechanism.
  4. Diagnose the location and type of a fault or discontinuity from a time-domain reflectometry (TDR) trace.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Decide when wave effects matter in a circuit and whether an interconnect must be modeled as a transmission line.
  2. Compare lumped-element, single-stub and quarter-wave matching for a given frequency and bandwidth, and justify a choice.
  3. Evaluate whether a PCB trace needs termination, given its length and the signal's rise time, and select a termination scheme.
  4. Judge whether the low-loss or good-conductor approximation is valid for a given line or medium.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a matching network for a given load and verify it in simulation or with a vector network analyzer.
  2. Design a termination scheme for a high-speed digital bus that meets a specified reflection budget.
  3. Build a Python model of a transmission-line circuit that plots standing-wave patterns or bounce-diagram transients.
  4. Capstone project: design, simulate and measure a microstrip interconnect with a matching network, including a TDR characterization and a short written design justification.

docs.title: Assessment (suggested)
docs.text: Component Weight Homework 20% Quizzes 10% Computational / lab projects (e.g., Smith chart, TDR measurements, field simulation) 15% Midterm exams (2) 30% Final exam 25%

docs.title: Learning Graph
docs.text:
The learning graph captures how concepts in Transmission Lines, Fields, and Waves depend on each other. It is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) — every concept has a path back to one or more foundational concepts that have no prerequisites.

Once the learning-graph-generator skill runs, this section will be populated with:

  • Course Description Assessment — quality review of course-description.md
  • Concept Enumeration — the ~200 concepts the book will cover
  • Concept Taxonomy — concepts grouped into 8–12 categories
  • Graph Quality Analysis — DAG structure, foundational and terminal nodes
  • Taxonomy Distribution — concept count per taxonomy category

Use the book-installer skill (option 23) to add an interactive graph viewer once learning-graph.json exists.

docs.title: Course Description Assessment
docs.text: Course: EE3601 — Transmission Lines, Fields, and Waves File assessed: docs/course-description.md Analyzer version: 0.05 Date: 2026-11-02 Previous score: 68/100 (2026-10-26)

docs.title: Overall Score: 100/100
docs.text:
Quality rating: Excellent — ready for learning graph generation.

The revision fixed both structural gaps found in the first assessment. The learning outcomes are now grouped under the six levels of the 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy, with four or five specific outcomes per level and a capstone project. A new "Topics Not Covered" section sets the course boundaries, and a "Tools" section names the software and lab equipment students use.

docs.title: Detailed Scoring Breakdown
docs.text: Element Points Earned Notes Title 5 5 "EE3601 — Transmission Lines, Fields, and Waves" is clear and descriptive. Target Audience 5 5 "Undergraduate, junior year." Prerequisites 5 5 Circuit analysis I and II, vector calculus, physics II; differential equations as a corequisite. Main Topics Covered 10 10 Twelve topics, each with a detailed list of subtopics. Topics Excluded 5 5 Seven explicit exclusions (antenna arrays, numerical EM, photonics, cavities, microwave networks, EMC, relativistic/quantum EM). Learning Outcomes Header 5 5 "After this course, students will be able to:" Remember Level 10 10 Five outcomes: constants, Maxwell's equations, Smith chart parts, line types, boundary conditions. Understand Level 10 10 Five outcomes: when circuit theory fails, standing waves, meaning of Maxwell's equations, plane-wave propagation, waveguides and radiation. Apply Level 10 10 Five outcomes: line calculations, Smith chart matching, Gauss/Ampère/Faraday, plane-wave reflection, waveguide cutoff. Analyze Level 10 10 Four outcomes: bounce diagrams, symmetry for Gaussian surfaces, separating loss and phase, TDR diagnosis. Evaluate Level 10 10 Four outcomes: when wave effects matter, choosing a matching method, termination decisions, validity of approximations. Create Level 10 10 Four outcomes, including a microstrip design–simulate–measure capstone. Descriptive Context 5 5 The course overview explains why circuit theory breaks down and why the course matters. Total 100 100

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
No element scored below full points.

One thing to check: the new outcomes and exclusions were drafted from the first assessment's suggestions, not written by the course author. They should be read for fit with how EE3601 is actually taught. In particular:

  • The capstone assumes access to a TDR and a vector network analyzer. If the lab has neither, change it to a simulation-only project.
  • "Microwave network theory beyond impedance matching" is excluded. If the course introduces S-parameters, remove that line from the exclusions.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
None are required to pass the gate. Optional refinements:

  1. If the assessment table changes (for example, a dedicated capstone weight), update it so it matches the Create-level outcomes.
  2. If specific textbooks are used (for example, Ulaby or Cheng), name them; this helps the reference-generator skill later.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
Factor Assessment Topic breadth 12 topics spanning circuits, statics, dynamics, and waves — excellent Topic depth Each topic lists 4–8 named subtopics — excellent Diversity of concept types Constants, definitions, laws, quantities, tools (Smith chart, TDR, VNA, Python), procedures (matching, termination), and design goals — excellent Boundaries Explicit exclusions keep the graph from drifting into neighboring subjects Estimated concept count About 260–330 concepts (≈ 20–25 per topic, plus tool and design concepts)

The Bloom-level outcomes now give the learning graph clear foundational concepts (Remember) and integrative goal concepts (Create and the capstone).

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).
